items.readable_text:
Content:
Let's consider the least-squares problem for the system

Content:
[MATH: A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}.]

Content:
We can use QR factorization to construct the least-squares solution of this system. Recall that finding the QR factorization of [MATH: A] means expressing [MATH: A] in the form

Content:
[MATH: A = QR,]

Content:
where

Content:
- [MATH: Q] has orthonormal columns, and
- [MATH: R] is an upper triangular matrix with positive entries on its main diagonal.

Content:
To see how QR factorization can be used to solve a least-squares problem, we first recall that the least-squares solution satisfies the normal equation

Content:
[MATH: A^T A \mathbf{x} = A^T \mathbf{b}.]

Content:
Substituting [MATH: A = QR,] we obtain

Content:
[MATH: A^{T}Ax|= A^{T}b; (QR)^{T}QRx|= (QR)^{T}b; R^{T}(Q^{T}Q)Rx|= R^{T}Q^{T}b.]

Content:
Since [MATH: Q] has orthonormal columns, we have [MATH: Q^T Q = I.] Therefore, the above equation becomes

Content:
[MATH: R^TR\mathbf{x} = R^TQ^T\mathbf{b}.]

Content:
Since [MATH: R^T] is invertible, pre-multiplying our equation by [MATH: (R^T)^{-1}] gives

Content:
[MATH: (R^{T})^{− 1} ⋅ R^{T}Rx|= (R^{T})^{− 1} ⋅ R^{T}Q^{T}b]
which simplifies as

Content:
[MATH: R \mathbf{x} = Q^T \mathbf{b}. \qquad\qquad (\ast)]

Content:
The least-squares solution [MATH: \hat{\mathbf x}] can now be found by solving this equation using back-substitution or row operations. This is usually the fastest way.

Content:
If we want an explicit formula for the least-squares solution, then we note that since [MATH: R] is invertible, pre-multiplying [MATH: (\ast)] by [MATH: R^{-1}] gives

Content:
[MATH: R^{− 1} ⋅ Rx|= R^{− 1} ⋅ Q^{T}b]

Content:
which simplifies as

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{x} = R^{-1} Q^T \mathbf{b}.]

Content:
The least-squares solution is unique if [MATH: A] has linearly independent columns.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION

The least-squares solution of [MATH: A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}] satisfies the normal equation

[MATH: A^T A\mathbf{x} = A^T\mathbf{b}.]

Substituting [MATH: A=QR,] we obtain

[MATH: A^{T}Ax|= A^{T}b; (QR)^{T}QRx|= (QR)^{T}b; R^{T}(Q^{T}Q)Rx|= R^{T}Q^{T}b.]

Since [MATH: Q] has orthonormal columns, it satisfies [MATH: Q^T Q = I,] and we get

[MATH: R^T R \mathbf{x} = R^T \! Q^T \mathbf{b}.]

Finally, since [MATH: R^T] is invertible, pre-multiplying by [MATH: (R^T)^{-1}] gives

[MATH: (R^{T})^{− 1} ⋅ R^{T}Rx|= (R^{T})^{− 1} ⋅ R^{T}Q^{T}b; R|x|= Q Tb.]

Therefore, the missing parts of the equation are [MATH: R] and [MATH: Q^T.]

Let's find the least-squares solution to [MATH: A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b},] where [MATH: A = QR,] and
[MATH: [− 1|1; 1|1]]

Content:
Previously, we showed that the normal equation corresponding to [MATH: A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},] where [MATH: A=QR,] can be reduced to

Content:
[MATH: R \mathbf{x} = Q^T \mathbf{b}.]

Content:
Substituting our matrices into this equation, we have

Content:
[MATH: (1)/(sqrt(2))[2|− 4; 0|3]^(⏞)^(R)x|= (1)/(sqrt(2))[− 1|1; 1|1]^(⏞)^(Q^{T})[2; 4]^(⏞)^(b); [2|− 4; 0|3]x|= [2; 6],]

Content:
which gives the system

Content:
[MATH: {2x_{1} − 4x_{2} = 2; 3x_{2} = 6.]

Content:
From the second equation, we get [MATH: x_2=2.] Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

Content:
[MATH: 2x_{1} − 4(2)|= 2; 2x_{1}|= 10; x_{1}|= 5.]

Content:
Therefore, the least-squares solution to [MATH: A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}] is [MATH: [5; 2]]

Given the QR decomposition [MATH: A=QR,] find the least-squares solution to [MATH: A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},] where
[MATH: [3|− 6; 6|2; 2|3]]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION

The least-squares solution of [MATH: A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}] satisfies the corresponding normal equation:

[MATH: A^T A\mathbf{x} = A^T\mathbf{b}]

Substituting [MATH: A=QR,] we obtain

[MATH: A^{T}Ax|= A^{T}b; (QR)^{T}QRx|= (QR)^{T}b; R^{T}(Q^{T}Q)Rx|= R^{T}Q^{T}b.]

Since [MATH: Q] has orthonormal columns, it satisfies [MATH: Q^T Q = I,] and we get

[MATH: R^T R \mathbf{x} = R^T \! Q^T \mathbf{b}.]

Finally, since [MATH: R^T] is invertible, pre-multiplying by [MATH: (R^T)^{-1}] gives

[MATH: (R^{T})^{− 1} ⋅ R^{T}Rx|= (R^{T})^{− 1} ⋅ R^{T}Q^{T}b; Rx|= Q^{T}b.]

Now, substituting our matrices, we have

[MATH: (1)/(7)[7|− 3; 0|2]^(⏞)^(R)x|= (1)/(7)[3|6|2; − 6|2|3]^(⏞)^(Q^{T})[0; 4; 2]^(⏞)^(b); [7|− 3; 0|2]x|= [28; 14],]

which gives the system

[MATH: {7x_{1} − 3x_{2} = 28; 2x_{2} = 14.]

From the second equation, we get [MATH: x_2=7.] Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

[MATH: 7x_{1} − 3(7)|= 28; 7x_{1}|= 49; x_{1}|= 7.]

Therefore, the least-squares solution to [MATH: A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b}] is [MATH: [7; 7]]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let's consider the least-squares problem for the system

Content:
[MATH: A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}.]

Content:

Content:
[MATH: A = QR,]

Content:
where

Content:
- [MATH: Q] has orthonormal columns, and
- [MATH: R] is an upper triangular matrix with positive entries on its main diagonal.

Content:
To see how QR factorization can be used to solve a least-squares problem, we first recall that the least-squares solution satisfies the normal equation

Content:
[MATH: A^T A \mathbf{x} = A^T \mathbf{b}.]

Content:
Substituting [MATH: A = QR,] we obtain

Content:
[MATH: A^{T}Ax|= A^{T}b; (QR)^{T}QRx|= (QR)^{T}b; R^{T}(Q^{T}Q)Rx|= R^{T}Q^{T}b.]

Content:
Since [MATH: Q] has orthonormal columns, we have [MATH: Q^T Q = I.] Therefore, the above equation becomes

Content:
[MATH: R^TR\mathbf{x} = R^TQ^T\mathbf{b}.]

Content:
Since [MATH: R^T] is invertible, pre-multiplying our equation by [MATH: (R^T)^{-1}] gives

Content:
[MATH: (R^{T})^{− 1} ⋅ R^{T}Rx|= (R^{T})^{− 1} ⋅ R^{T}Q^{T}b]
which simplifies as

Content:
[MATH: R \mathbf{x} = Q^T \mathbf{b}. \qquad\qquad (\ast)]

Content:
The least-squares solution [MATH: \hat{\mathbf x}] can now be found by solving this equation using back-substitution or row operations. This is usually the fastest way.

Content:
If we want an explicit formula for the least-squares solution, then we note that since [MATH: R] is invertible, pre-multiplying [MATH: (\ast)] by [MATH: R^{-1}] gives

[MATH: (R^{T})^{− 1} ⋅ R^{T}Rx|= (R^{T})^{− 1} ⋅ R^{T}Q^{T}b; Rx|= Q^{T}b.]
